strengths: Well-motivated and novel problem formulation: reconstructing a full hyperspectral cube from a single filterless grayscale capture through a single flat optic is a genuinely minimalist, unsolved scenario, and the paper convincingly establishes the first feasibility demonstration (concept & feasibility contribution type).

Technically sound core idea: patch-based conditional diffusion training combined with inference-time cross-patch guidance derived from the physically modeled PSF elegantly resolves the patch-ambiguity problem caused by an extended-support blur kernel, and the least-squares per-patch rescaling is a sensible fix for the scale ambiguity from max-normalization.

Strong empirical results: 2.86 dB PSNR improvement over the next best (retrained) baseline in the filterless setting, consistent gains in SSIM and SAM, and additional validation in Bayer+optic and Bayer-only settings; ablations (patch size, stride, rescale, guidance) clearly isolate where the gains come from.

Thorough analysis beyond headline metrics: PSF-design comparison across eight metalens designs yields actionable insight (spectral/spatial encoding trade-off; best filterless designs differ from prior RGB-mosaic designs), saliency analysis shows the network implicitly learns the PSF and shift-invariance, and cross-dataset generalization (CAVE, ICVL, Harvard) at higher resolutions without finetuning supports the 'any resolution' claim.

Useful uncertainty quantification: multi-sample spectral variance correlates with true error (Pearson 0.80) and widens appropriately in cross-distribution cases, a capability none of the baselines offer.

Reproducibility support is good: full model configuration, pseudo-code for guided sampling, runtime tables, noise-robustness study, PSF design theory with source code availability, and clear documentation of the simulation forward model.

Honest scoping: the paper consistently presents results as simulation-based and identifies practical limits (patch size lower bound, guidance iterations as computational bottleneck, adaptive compute as future work).
weaknesses: No real hardware captures: all experiments use simulated measurements from a wave-optics forward model. The gap between the idealized shift-invariant PSF model and a physically fabricated metalens (calibration error, PSF non-idealities, alignment, sensor quantum efficiency, Poisson/dark noise, vignetting) is not empirically bridged; the noise study covers only additive Gaussian noise, which weakens the practical claims of enabling a 'new class of imagers'.

Baseline comparisons are somewhat favorable to the authors: competing models were designed for better-conditioned, full-field tasks and had to be adapted, and full comparisons are confined to 256×256 resized images; there is no baseline that uses the known PSF as an explicit prior (e.g., model-based/unrolling methods using the measurement operator on patches), which would more fairly isolate whether the advantage comes from diffusion guidance or from conditioning information the baselines cannot exploit.

Computational cost is significant and the trade-off is only partially explored: 20 guidance iterations take ~22s for a 256×256 HSI on an RTX 3090, and accuracy degrades substantially without guidance; scaling to genuinely high-resolution fields (e.g., 1280×1280 with 400 patches in parallel) is demonstrated on out-of-distribution data but runtime/memory at that scale is not reported.

The guidance is applied to patch states xt with the loss gradient computed through the stitched full-field forward model; potential failure modes (guidance overshoot, per-patch scale constants treated without gradient tracking, sensitivity to the number of guidance iterations shown in Fig. 8) are acknowledged but the robustness of the method to these hyperparameters across datasets is not deeply characterized.

Some claims are stated more strongly than the evidence: 'first high-quality results' and 'first patch-based reconstruction with blur kernel larger than patch size' are plausible but rely on an informal survey of adjacent literature, and the real-vs-fake object discrimination demo (CAVE) is a small, qualitative 5-scene experiment.

The measurement/HSI patch pairs come from a single primary dataset (ARAD1K) for the main comparisons; dependence of the local-optical-cue conclusion on this dataset's spectral diversity is not fully explored in-distribution.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuinely new and minimalist inverse problem—reconstructing a 31-channel HSI from a same-pixel-count grayscale measurement captured through a single flat optic—and provides what appears to be the first working solution, which is a meaningful contribution to computational imaging.

The core technical idea is well-motivated and clearly articulated: patch-based diffusion training for data efficiency, combined with a physics-grounded cross-patch guidance term that enforces full-field measurement consistency via the PSF-based forward operator. This elegantly addresses the patch-ambiguity problem caused by the extended-support blur kernel (Fig. 2).

The experimental evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: comparison against eight trained baselines (Table 1), ablations of patch size, stride, rescaling, and guidance (Table 2), a systematic study of eight PSF/lens designs (Table 3), runtime analysis (Fig. 8, Table 4), noise robustness (supplement), cross-dataset and cross-resolution generalization without fine-tuning (Sec. 4.5), and an interpretable saliency analysis (Sec. 4.4) that empirically validates that the model learns the PSF structure.

The per-pixel uncertainty estimates with a reported 0.80 correlation to true error, plus the scale-ambiguity analysis in the supplement (Sec. 10), show real technical care rather than just reporting metrics.

Writing and figure quality are generally good; the method (Eqs. 4-8, Algorithm 1) is described at a level of detail that supports reproducibility, and the metalens design theory in the supplement adds value.
weaknesses: The entire evaluation is simulation-only. All measurements are rendered with an idealized shift-invariant, wavelength-dependent PSF (Eq. 1) computed under simplifying assumptions (normal incidence, fixed 5 µm pixels, 1 cm distance). Claims of enabling 'a new class of snapshot hyperspectral imagers' rest entirely on this simulation; real metalens systems exhibit field-varying PSFs, manufacturing errors, misalignment, and calibration error that are never tested. Given the paper's framing as a camera design paper, the absence of even a single physically captured measurement is the most consequential weakness.

The baseline comparison conditions are not fully symmetric: the proposed model trains on patches and applies test-time guidance using knowledge of the exact forward operator, while the eight baselines are full-field models trained on 256×256 measurements with modified forward operators ('minimal modifications'). It is unclear whether the baselines were given comparable access to the measurement operator, and some (e.g., deep unfolding methods like DAUHST/In2Set) are architecture-coupled to their original operator, which may disadvantage them. The 2.86 dB margin may therefore partly reflect methodological asymmetry rather than a strict superiority of patch diffusion.

Practical runtime is significant: ~22 s for a single 256×256×31 reconstruction at 20 guidance iterations on an RTX 3090, and accuracy keeps improving up to 60 iterations (68 s). The paper's headline of 'any resolution' is undermined by the O(n² log n) guidance cost and the fact that all quantitative claims are made at 256×256.

The claim that 'local optical cues are sufficient to capture full spectral information' is supported only on ARAD1K-like natural scenes; cross-dataset results already show measurable degradation, and the method assumes the diffusion prior generalizes. Spectral recovery from chromatic aberration alone is fundamentally prior-dependent, and the paper does not probe failure modes (e.g., spectrally flat or metameric scenes, saturated regions).

The guidance procedure is somewhat heuristic: the per-patch least-squares rescaling (Eq. 4) excludes gradients 'for efficiency' at an unquantified accuracy cost, the number of repeated guidance steps is hand-tuned, and no analysis is given of when the guidance could converge to measurement-consistent but incorrect solutions—an important concern in a severely ill-posed problem.

Robustness testing is limited to additive Gaussian noise; real sensors with a filterless, highly light-efficient design would raise different noise and dynamic-range considerations (partly acknowledged for Poisson noise, but untested).

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem formulation: reconstructing a full HSI from a single grayscale snapshot captured with only a flat diffractive optic and a filterless sensor with equal pixel count is a genuinely minimalist, unsolved scenario, and the paper convincingly positions it against CASSI-style and RGB-to-HSI systems.

Technically sound and clearly described method: the combination of patch-based conditional diffusion training with physics-grounded cross-patch PSF guidance (including a non-iterative least-squares per-patch scale correction) is an elegant solution to the patch-ambiguity problem caused by an extended-support measurement kernel. The guidance algorithm (Eqs. 4-7, Algorithm 1) is fully specified and reproducible.

Strong empirical evidence: 2.86 dB PSNR improvement over nine strong baselines retrained from scratch under identical conditions, careful ablations (patch size, stride, rescaling, guidance), runtime analysis, and a principled lens-design study across eight PSFs that yields actionable design insights (T4/R1 preferred over heavier-mixing R2/R3).

Beyond accuracy metrics, the paper provides uncertainty estimates that correlate well with true error (Pearson 0.80), a perturbation-saliency analysis showing the network implicitly learns the physical PSF, and cross-dataset/cross-resolution generalization (ICVL, Harvard, CAVE) without finetuning - a convincing demonstration that the model captures shift-invariant optics rather than dataset shortcuts.

Supplementary material is thorough: noise-robustness experiments, pseudo-code, full optical design theory (metalens construction, Fresnel propagation), and complete training/model configuration support reproducibility, with stated code release.
weaknesses: All results are simulation-only. For a paper whose headline claim is a 'new class of snapshot hyperspectral imagers,' there is no physical capture, no real metalens prototype, and no measured data. Real-world factors (PSF model mismatch, fabrication errors, sensor calibration, alignment, photon noise characteristics beyond the Gaussian model tested) could substantially degrade performance, and the claim of 'first demonstration' should be tempered accordingly.

The forward model assumes a perfectly known, shift-invariant, wavelength-dependent PSF used both to render measurements and to guide sampling. This circularity means the method's success partly rests on the fidelity of the wave-optics simulator; sensitivity to PSF estimation error is not studied.

The baselines (SST, MST, DAUHST, HDNet, etc.) were designed for better-conditioned CASSI/RGB tasks and are adapted to the new operator; while retraining them fairly is commendable, none is designed for this ill-posed filterless setting, so the magnitude of the improvement over purpose-built alternatives is uncertain.

Guidance is the main computational bottleneck (roughly linear cost growth, e.g., ~22-68 s per reconstruction at 20-60 iterations on a 256x256 image), and the method requires 10 samples for uncertainty. Scalability to the promised high-resolution 'any resolution' regime (e.g., 1280x1280 with hundreds of patches and full-field convolution guidance) is analyzed only asymptotically (O(n^2 log n)) rather than measured.

Uncertainty validity is assessed via Pearson correlation with MSE, which does not establish proper calibration (e.g., coverage or CRPS); generative diffusion uncertainty can be overconfident in OOD regimes, and only informal evidence (wider uncertainty cross-dataset) is given.
Minor: the supplementary Bayer analysis acknowledges that results do not model spatial demosaicing, so the reported Bayer numbers slightly overstate what a real single-capture system would achieve.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem formulation: reconstructing H×W×31 hyperspectral images from a single filterless panchromatic snapshot via a single flat optic is a minimalist, largely underexplored scenario, and the paper convincingly positions it against CASSI/filter-based systems (e.g., light throughput, no mosaic subsampling).

Technically sound core idea: patch-based conditional diffusion combined with inference-time PSF-guidance that stitches patch predictions and enforces full-field measurement consistency elegantly addresses the cross-patch ambiguity caused by PSF support comparable to patch size; the per-patch scale recovery via least squares (Eq. 3) is a clean solution to the patch normalization ambiguity.

Extensive and convincing evidence: large gains over nine retrained baselines on ARAD1K (+2.86 dB PSNR), cross-dataset generalization (ICVL, Harvard, CAVE) without finetuning, a fabricated metalens prototype with real captures (31.2 dB PSNR), plus a CASSI benchmark experiment showing the framework generalizes to other forward models (35.46 dB, exceeding MST-L).

Insightful analysis: patch-size-vs-PSF ablations, saliency maps that recover PSF structure, PSF design comparison showing optimal designs differ from RGB-mosaic designs, metameric scene discrimination, and controlled checkerboard failure-mode analysis.

Well-validated uncertainty estimates: per-pixel variance strongly correlates with reconstruction error in both simulation (r=0.80) and experiment (r=0.69), and per-channel analysis plus the CASSI uncertainty-filtered metrics demonstrate practical utility.

Thorough experimental detail and honest limitations section: prototype calibration, LoRA sim-to-real finetuning, noise robustness, PSF shift-invariance validation, and clearly stated limitations (homogeneous regions, lack of global context propagation) strengthen scientific credibility.
weaknesses: Baseline comparisons, while extensive, are against models designed for better-conditioned tasks (CASSI, RGB-to-HSI) adapted to the filterless setting; there is no evidence the adapted baselines are optimal for this regime, so the magnitude of the reported gap may overstate the true advantage, though the UNet-Regress control partially mitigates this concern.

Runtime is substantial: ~22 s/scene at 256×256 but up to ~52 minutes for higher-resolution scenes; the proposed scheduling and distillation mitigations are discussed but not fully validated, limiting practical applicability claims for interactive use.

The guidance loss (Eq. 4) enforces consistency against the noiseless measurement while real measurements are noisy (robustness is addressed via training-time noise augmentation, but the mismatch between the guidance objective and noisy observations is not analyzed in the main text).

Some hyperparameters and design choices (e.g., R1 lens hand-tuned, guidance iteration count reduced to 10 on experimental scenes 'to avoid over-guiding') risk implicit tuning; a stricter held-out protocol for these choices would strengthen the claims.

Uncertainty is evaluated only via Pearson correlation with squared error; no proper calibration metrics (e.g., coverage of credible intervals), so the uncertainty maps are validated as error predictors but not as calibrated posteriors.

Experimental validation uses only 15 tabletop scenes (6 finetune/8 test) with approximate homography registration; while carefully handled, the experimental evidence is thin relative to the simulation study, and the shift-invariance validation uses a different physical sample than the imaging lens.

Minor inconsistencies (e.g., no-guidance PSNR reported as 32.32 in Tab. 1 vs 32.2/34.67 in Tab. 2 discussion) and heavy reliance on the supplement for key details slightly reduce clarity of the main paper.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely novel and largely unexplored problem setting — reconstructing a 31-channel hyperspectral image from a single filterless panchromatic measurement captured through a single flat optic (metalens) — and clearly articulates why this is harder and different from existing snapshot HSI (CASSI, Bayer-filtered, diffractive+filter systems).

The core technical contribution is substantive: a conditional patch diffusion model combined with inference-time global PSF-consistency guidance (with closed-form per-patch scale recovery) that makes patch-based diffusion viable even when the degradation kernel spans the entire patch. The claim that no prior patch-based approach handles such large kernels is well supported by the ablations (e.g., 32-pixel patches drop from 33.27 to 29.27 dB without guidance).

Evidence is unusually comprehensive for this type of paper: (i) comparison against 8–9 strong baselines retrained on the rendered measurements (+2.86 dB PSNR over the next best); (ii) a UNet-regression ablation isolating the effect of the diffusion prior; (iii) patch size / guidance / normalization ablations; (iv) a systematic PSF design study across 8 lenses; (v) cross-dataset generalization (ICVL, Harvard, CAVE) including a metameric-scene result; (vi) a fabricated metalens prototype with careful PSF characterization, shift-invariance validation, spectral calibration, LoRA finetuning, and real experimental results (31.20 dB PSNR); and (vii) a supplementary CASSI benchmark result exceeding MST-L.

Interpretability and uncertainty analyses (saliency maps mirroring the PSF, per-channel uncertainty-error correlation of 0.80/0.69) add scientific insight beyond raw benchmark numbers, and the uncertainty-based pixel selection on CASSI is a practical added value.

Limitations are candidly and thoroughly discussed (homogeneous-region failure modes, lack of global context propagation, runtime), with a controlled synthetic experiment probing the texture-scale dependency. The paper is clearly written and well organized; the experimental pipeline (fabrication, calibration, alignment tolerances) is documented to a reproducible level.
weaknesses: All quantitative baseline comparisons in the main text are against methods designed for better-conditioned problems (CASSI or Bayer/RGB inputs) retrained on the filterless task; there is no prior method designed for this setting, so the 'surpassing by 2.86 dB' claim is relative to retrained baselines rather than purpose-built competitors. The authors acknowledge this, and the supplementary CASSI experiment partially mitigates it, but it remains the weakest evidentiary link.

Reconstruction is slow: ~22 s per ARAD1K scene and up to 52 minutes per scene at higher resolutions, even with the quadratic guidance schedule. The paper offers mitigation paths (distillation) but they are not demonstrated, so real-time or even near-real-time use remains speculative.

Real-system validation is limited: only 15 tabletop scenes, finetuned on 6 of them, evaluated on 8, with approximately registered views via homographies and residual misalignment absorbed by random offset augmentation. The sim-to-real bridge is credible but the diversity of real scenes (indoor tabletop, no outdoor/dynamic scenes) is narrow relative to the generality implied by the framing.

The method fundamentally requires scene texture at the PSF scale (uniform regions are unrecoverable), which is a significant practical constraint on real-world deployment; the failure-mode analysis is appreciated but this limitation bounds the applicability of the proposed camera class.

Uncertainty quantification is empirical (seed variance) rather than a calibrated posterior; correlation with MSE (0.69–0.80) is useful but a formal treatment (e.g., calibration curves, coverage) would strengthen the claim.

Runtime figures are given on specific GPUs with gradient checkpointing, but the memory footprint for very large images (e.g., 480 parallel patches) is not fully characterized, which complicates assessment of the scalability claims.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem formulation: reconstructing a 31-channel HSI from a single filterless grayscale snapshot through a flat diffractive optic is a severely ill-posed and largely unexplored setting; the paper clearly articulates why prior patch-based methods fail here (PSF support comparable to patch size) and what makes their approach work.

The core technical contribution—training a conditional patch diffusion model on small data and synchronizing patch predictions at inference via guidance from the physical forward model (with closed-form per-patch scale recovery)—is elegant, well-specified (including pseudo-code and normalization details), and demonstrably effective: ~2.9 dB PSNR gain over adapted baselines, with ablations (Tab. 2) cleanly isolating the role of guidance, patch size, and rescaling.

Unusually thorough empirical evidence for this area: eight different baseline models retrained on the rendered measurements, an RGB-Bayer variant, cross-dataset generalization (ICVL/Harvard/CAVE without finetuning), PSF design comparison across eight lenses, saliency analysis showing the model implicitly learns the PSF structure, generalization to CASSI in the supplement, and a failure-mode analysis for homogeneous regions.

Strong systems contribution: a fabricated TiO2 metalens prototype with careful experimental characterization (measured PSFs, shift-invariance validation, spectral calibration) and LoRA-based sim-to-real finetuning, achieving 31.2 dB PSNR on real captures—moving well beyond a simulation-only study.

Honest limitations section (homogeneous regions, no global context propagation) and a useful, validated per-pixel uncertainty estimate (Pearson 0.80 simulated / 0.69 experimental), which no baseline provides.
weaknesses: No baseline is specifically designed for the filterless setting, so the comparison necessarily adapts models from better-conditioned tasks; the concurrent SLM-based filterless approach (Liu et al. [29]) is discussed but not empirically compared, leaving the strongest available apples-to-apples comparison absent.

Reconstruction is slow (22 s per ARAD1K scene, up to 52 min for high-resolution scenes), and the uncertainty estimate requires N full sampling runs; while the paper outlines mitigations (quadratic guidance schedules, distillation), these are not fully validated.

The contribution is a system-level integration of known components (patch diffusion, DPS-style guidance, LoRA finetuning, metalens optics); the novelty is in the combination and the demonstration rather than a fundamentally new algorithm, which some reviewers may weigh differently.
Uncertainty–error correlation, while consistent, is moderate (0.69 in the real system), and uncertainty maps are only validated against MSE; calibration properties (e.g., coverage) are not analyzed.

The experimental evaluation relies on only 15 tabletop scenes with imperfect homography registration, and 6 of them are used for finetuning; the real-system quantitative results rest on a small test set of 8 scenes, and the reference camera's own limitations are not quantified.
